Is the game biz sustainable for the average indie dev?
Two ways to approach the question. Also: game discovery news & this week’s Show.
Simon Carless
Sep 16, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
We’re back, and thinking carefully about a more existential question in today’s main newsletter story. (Do we want to do this? Not really. Should we do it so that everyone is on the same page, for better or worse? Probably!)
Before we start, you know YouTuber Any Austin from videos like ‘ Where Do Hyrule’s Rivers Go? ’ and ‘ Do Grand Theft Auto V’s Power Lines Connect To Anything? ’ Well, he’s continuing this line of in-game ecosystem research with his latest video featuring Cyberpunk 2077: ‘ What Is Night City's Unemployment Rate? ’ (Bravo.)

Game disco news: welcome back, Happy Wheels…
Let’s start out by checking out the latest game platform & discovery news from across the video game-verse:
Looking at GDCo Pro's estimates of 'trending' unreleased Steam games by 'new wishlists in the last 7 days' (above), a surprise is Flash ragdoll physics 2D game Happy Wheels (#1) , coming to Steam 15 years post-launch (!). At #2 when we ran this, but out now, Dimraeth is an isometric co-op fantasy RPG with much depth.
Other newly trending titles? Furry wolf-children making sim (?!) Family Time (#6), which picked up ~70k wishlists after its announce. Gritty open-world survival-er The Dead We Knew (#7) is also adding interest. And cute/realistic zombie survival game Zeverland (interesting combo!) made it to #10.
Valve’s Steam Frame is now officially unveiled , with a USD $1,059 (256 GB) and USD $1,200 (1TB) price point, and a YouTube video from Valve takes you through the standalone VR device (which also connects to a PC!) This BBC review approximates general reception: “The hardware is excellent - a light device which feels comfortable to wear and is packed with clever technology… but it comes at a high price.”
Heavily rumored, the Triple-I Initiative streaming showcase is now happening twice per year , and October 8th is the next one, with “35+ announcements with back-to-back trailers of world premieres, gameplay reveals, launch dates [&] demos.” Teaser trailer here , and reveals from Dave the Diver, Risk of Rain 2 & more are promised.
Roblox Developers Conference had a huge announce, with the keynote revealing : “Soon, creators will have the option to make their games available as standalone apps across mobile, PC, and consoles, with Roblox powering the technology and services underneath.” (This pivot seems early, with scant details besides web play in 2026 & offline modes by mid-2027 - we’ll see if/how it interacts with Steam…)
Other ambitious Roblox things: RDC’s keynote also confirmed Roblox engine improvements to enable “2D and puzzle games” more easily, as well as Roblox Wallet , “a creator earnings account Roblox said lets creators earn directly in real currency, get paid automatically each business day”, and also a Roblox debit card.
Steam (and other online platforms!) have “ implemented age verification measures for Australian users , affecting titles that carry a local age rating of R18+”, and you’ll need to link select credit cards for it to work. (This came “ in the wake of changes to Australia’s online safety code made earlier in 2026” , and appears mandatory.)
In as much as Blizzcon is related to Xbox’s platform success, you can check out the big announces here , inc. a Starcraft shooter for 2030 and Diablo V in 2029. (Also: after adding CD Projekt games, Battle.net says they’ll be selective re: more games: “We're obviously not out there trying to do the Steam or Epic Game Store thing.” )
The latest PlayStation Plus Game Catalog additions for September (for higher PS+ tiers) have a pretty nice diversity of titles, including RuneScape: Dragonwilds, WWE 2K26, Ball x Pit, and Date Everything! (There’s also cult-ier titles like Slitterhead, Ninja Gaiden: Ragebound & Dungeons of Hinterberg.)
According to Circana's Future of Insights for Video Games Consumer Survey , “cost is becoming a stronger driver of US cancellations to Xbox Game Pass Essential, PS Plus Essential and Nintendo Switch Online” , with ‘couldn’t justify the cost’ reason for canceling up 4-10% from Q1, hitting at least 40% for all three.
Microlinks: there’s speculation that you might need a trailer to appear in Steam Discovery Queue (whether or not, it’s good to have one!); August’s top grossing mobile games include Honor Of Kings, Gossip Harbor & PUBG Mobile; some data on Towerpunk’s reveal to >4k Steam wishlists , good thanks to a viral trailer.

Finding creators is a grind. You email 200 YouTubers, hear back from six, and hand out keys with no idea what happens next. Creators.gg puts your game in front of 20,000+ creators looking for their next title.
Listing is free and takes under 10 minutes. Start with a key drop and auto-approval rules, then scale as far as you want: CPM campaigns, performance-based rewards, or a full Creator Battle Pass .
100+ programs are live, from first-time key drops to EWC’s $2M creator program. Start free today .
Is the game biz.. sustainable for the average indie?
January 2026’s top Steam paid releases (lifetime revenue) pre GDCo estimates - we also dumped the entire chart onto Google Sheets , if you want to analyze it.
When i went on Mike Rose & Rami Ismail’s ‘wide-ranging’ (lol!) games podcast Mike & Rami Are Still Here , I was reminded that there are many possible ways to view the game biz. GameDiscoverCo tends to hover over the PC/console ecosystem like The Watcher from the Fantastic Four , finding & analyzing the games that are doing well.
But you can also zoom down to the more human level: what should the average person do? And that’s exactly what Rami asked me at the end of the podcast : " If you’re an indie right now, the question I get most is like, is this worth it right now? Right? Like, should we?” And that’s a 100% valid question that we’ve, well, mainly skirted…
Answer #1: what the data says…
So we’re going to answer it two ways: a data-led answer (which is what you’d expect from us), and then quote from what we actually said during the podcast, which is a bit more ‘feels’ -based . Let’s start with indie game-ish data - which goes a bit like this:
Let’s say you spent USD $500k of your own money to make your game: no publisher, but you get all the upside. If you released that game on Steam in January 2026 (above) , you’d need to be one of the 16 games of 1,230 (1.3%) that grossed >$1m LTD to have made $550k+ net back (after refunds, chargebacks, Valve’s 30%), and now be profitable, w/ongoing cashflow.
Let’s say you spent USD $500k of a publisher’s money to make a game: it depends on your recoup, but we’d think that only ~7 of the games (0.6%) released in Jan would have recouped fully by now at ‘normal’ rates. These are not exciting headline numbers.
So that gets to the following questions: how many games do you need in your catalog to build up an acceptable ‘long tail’ for continued operations, if you’re self-pub? And how much cushion do you need in your bank account between publishing deals , if you can’t rely on royalties alone to fund your indie? (Given external $ got pinched.)
Maybe you can argue January is a slow month, and we shouldn’t be using it . (It’s true that some months in 2026 have more like 20-30 new games grossing >$1m.) You can also note that some (but not many non-cozy) indie games will also add revenue on console platforms at minimal extra cost . But it doesn’t shift the fundamental math(s).
What this says to us is: even at a game funding number ($500k) that some readers will say is radically too low, and some too high, there’s indications that you need to be hitting home runs to make the ‘new PC games’ market work for you at all. (Even at $100k budget, only 80 of the 1,230 (6.5%) would be breakeven net, if self-published.)
Answer #2: what the gut says…
Then there’s what I said on the podcast, referencing my ‘I’ve been in the biz for 30 years’ newsletter where I accidentally outed myself as a dinosaur (above) . As I joked with Mike & Rami, there’s no 10km-wide asteroid heading for the game biz . But “there’s also no - in my view - return to the old days.” Really, what I see for indies - and what I said - is:
There’s going to be a continuation of ‘so many people can make video games’. Many of those people are making games semi-professionally, or doing it just after they left school, or in a low-cost situation or locality. In many cases, this may not be a disadvantage for their popularity.
So for better or worse, if you want a long full-time career in games: if you don’t have a game that’s done well, that you own and have continued revenue from , it’s going to be much trickier in the future. Not impossible, but way trickier.
I think there are great, successful games out there. I’m kind of a glass half-full kind of guy. There are good things going on in the PC/console game space , and projects that impress and wow me every week.
But I don’t deny on the individual level , especially if everyone needs a salary and you’re working with multiple people on your team, it’s rough, and it’s going to continue to be rough …
I concluded: “I think people have to find ways to make games less conventionally. I’m excited about the increasing number of games doing well overall. But it’s true that the vast majority (by %) of new games in 2026 aren’t going to perform commercially…”
So: the biz works, if you’re a) a publisher with a strong overall catalog, or b) a compact dev team who’s created something notable from a lower cost base. (I think of games like single-player, moddable lo-fi Battlefield riff Ravenfield , which my 10-year old loves, and GDCo estimates has grossed $15m since 2017…)
Yet overall, as a smaller indie, I think you need to understand the odds. And - I’m sorry, I think this is the second time I’ve quoted Kenny Rogers in this newsletter - “ Know when to hold 'em , know when to fold 'em , know when to walk away, know when to run.”
GameDiscoverCo Show: why’s Xbox going Kojima?
Just in time for the newsletter, we have The GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante talking game discovery trends - sub to the podcast via Apple Music , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
This time, we talk about how Xbox is doubling down on Hideo Kojima after PlayStation dropped Physint, Ubisoft's move away from its Steam launcher, smaller Steam games getting better personalized visibility, and CliffyB talking about how AAA should 'faceplant for a while' in this new PC/console game creation paradigm.

author: James Batchelor

Before Balacho launched, we knew we had something special. Nobody knows how special that could have been, but there was such a buzz about the game, such an excitement about it. And we all had a little wildest dream forecast for how the game might do, and we were all low on how it did.
We are really proud of that, but the 15% is really important too, because if you only did things that were safe and only did things that were going to be profitable or any things that could work, you don't take as many risks. And I don't think indie publishing is about that.
I think indie publishing and indie development is about taking risks. It's about having an idea that people just genuinely don't quite see how, but it's become phenomenal and captured people. So maybe 85% is a really nice number. Maybe 70% would be brilliant too.

Hello there and welcome to The Game Business Show. This edition is sponsored by HelpShift, a Keyword Studios platform. Now HelpShift says that players already trust AI to help them. The problem is that most AI in gaming wasn't built to. According to the company, 66% of players are comfortable with AI handling their issue first as long as there's
a human behind it. 74% want it resolved without leaving the game, and 58% will quit over a bad support experience. Now studios agree as well, 80% see AI becoming the default for player support. Their worry isn't AI, it's AI that doesn't understand games. That's the Gap Keyword Studio's AI-native platform HelpShift was built to close.
One AI agent can handle a lot, but it can't handle everything. A billing query and a self-harm disclosure can't share the same tone, rules or guardrails. Care AI lets you build specialist AI agents, each one of them an expert, where it matters, each handing off to a human when it should. You can find out more at HelpShift.com,
plus there are more details, including a video, in the newsletter attached with this show. Speaking of this show, let's get on with it. This week we're talking to leading indie publisher Playstack, which is probably best known for its 2024 smash hit, Palatro, but is also responsible for games like Mortal Shell,
Raccoine, and it's publishing the upcoming Star Trek Outposts Unknown. Now Playstack celebrated its 10th anniversary this year, and it's done so by changing owners. It was acquired by Integrated Media Company, the owner of Fandom and GameSpot. When it valued Playstack at 125 million pounds.
So we thought this would be a great excuse to catch up with Playstack CEO Harvey Elliott. Now what you're going to get is actually two interviews because we spoke to Playstack before its IMC acquisition. So part one is going to be about Bellatro and indie publishing and the market in general.
While we'll have a quick mini chat about its new owners after that. Enjoy. Hello, Harvey. Welcome to the show. Thank you, Chris. Nice to be here. You know what? I haven't caught up with you since Bellatro.
S2
SPEAKER 2
Which is actually two years ago. I know.
S1
SPEAKER 1
Two years, three months. Which is just upsetting, but what a seismic release. What a huge success. Has that changed PlayStack?
S2
SPEAKER 2
A little bit, yes. I mean, PlayStack for what we do, what we set out to do, isn't any different to when we set out 10 years ago, but When you have something like Ballatro happen and, you know, it's a once in a lifetime type of game. The reach has had the phenomenon that it is.
It's just very validating and it makes everyone feel Like what we do is worth it, that it really matters. And we're so proud of every game that we publish. You know, we genuinely put our heart and soul into every title. But when one like that just sort of catches and catches players in
a way you didn't know it was going to, and just the reach has had, the success it's had, it's very validating and it makes us feel very positive and it gives a little spring in our step. But it doesn't change the steps we're taking. We just bounce a little bit more as we take them.

SPEAKER 1
Certain games give publishers a, unintentionally maybe like a brand or a vibe, or this is the publisher, you know, Team17 because of worms for ages, or this is the publisher that does sort of quirky multiplayer games. Devolver because of maybe Hotline Miami is the one that does it.
It's not true because they do lots of different types of games. But have you found that you're getting approached by certain developers who make certain types of games?
S2
SPEAKER 2
Well, definitely. So it's true to an extent. I think on the inside of those companies, I don't know that Team17 feel like the Worms company or Devolver feel like the Hotline Miami company, because they know all the other things they do, but you can't necessarily help how people will perceive you.
And for a lot of people, the only thing they will know PlayStack for is Balatro. Hopefully, the nurse for Abiotic Factor, the nurse for Recoin, the nurse for other titles. And actually, to that point, Recoin's a really good example. There's no way we would have been publishing Recoin if we hadn't published Balatro, because...
They saw us publish Balatro and, oh my goodness, they've got to publish this. They probably were inspired by Balatro. So Recoin probably only existed because Balatro existed. And because Recoin existed and we'd published Balatro, they had to bring it to us. So it created, I think, Recoin in that way.
And we've got a surprising number of those sort of parlor roguelike games being pitched to us and approached, and we've got a couple more coming out. So yes, it's sort of created a sort of a theme within the games, but there's still a very small proportion of what we do in that sort of category of game.
And really, there only is one Balatro. We have other games that sort of capture some of that sentiment, but not in the same way. Yes, it changes what we've pitched. Yes, it changes how some people might perceive us. But inside, we don't feel like that's all we do.
S1
SPEAKER 1
So in 2016, a story that I would have definitely have edited was when PlayStack was announced and it was a Gamescom, I think. It was a Gamescom edition of MCD anyway it was in. And you said at the time you wanted to fix the word publisher. Is that mission complete?
S2
SPEAKER 2
I don't think it's ever complete, but I think we made some really good steps to that, yes. And I think It can never be complete because there are so many publishers out there that mean, that publishing means so many things to so many people.
But what we set out to do, I think we do deliver that and I really feel very proud of it. What we try and do is we say every game is unique, every development team is unique, and they will have things that they all need, but in different proportions. Some need funding, some need directions, some need guidance.
None of them need to be told how to make the game they know. That's the one thing, you know, we're very aware of. But they still need help and support and structure. And champions, and people who believe in them, and people who can find audiences for their games.
And I think those are missions that we do accomplish for our developers and our partners. So I do think that's definitely working. I think there's always more we can do, and there's always lessons we take from every game. Even hits like Balatro, there are things we could do differently for the next time around.
So I think it's always going to be a

work in progress, but I do feel like we made some really positive steps, yes. You teased something there. What did you learn from, what did you learn from Balatro?

Beyond Balatro and taking risks: Why Playstack doesn’t want a 100% hit rate
We speak to CEO Harvey Elliott as the indie publisher enters a new era under new ownership
James Batchelor
Sep 16, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Playstack’s Harvey Elliott on…
The impact of Balatro
Its 85% hit rate
Playstack’s new owners
Taking risks
Indie publisher Playstack is celebrating its tenth anniversary, and yet the company’s name has arguably only been on everyone’s lips for a couple of years – thanks largely to poker-themed roguelike deckbuilder Balatro.
As with so many indie breakouts, the 2024 smash hit seemed to come from nowhere but Playstack CEO and founder Harvey Elliott says his team were confident long before the name ‘Balatro’ was making headlines.
“We knew we had something special,” he tells The Game Business Show . “Nobody knows how special that could have been, but there was such a buzz about the game, such excitement. We all had our dream forecasts for how the game might do – and we were all low.
“The game built the fervor for itself and we just gave it a voice, gave it an audience and some reach. But the game just really captivated imaginations and it made people feel very smart when you’re getting really good at combos and trying to work out the right way to put your jokers or prepare your deck.”
Balatro not only provided Playstack with great success but also with valuable lessons; for example, Elliott believes the company could have created “a different kinds of moment” if it had released on PC, consoles and mobile simultaneously (as opposed to the latter arriving several months later).
“Those sort of lessons, like the launch planning, timing the game release, and getting it out there, and just little things about when you submit a game on multiple platforms all at once... We’ve done more complicated things since because of Balatro, but we didn’t necessarily do them all with Balatro first time. A multi-SKU release is complicated, especially with a solo dev driving the creative and driving the game.”

66% of players are comfortable with AI handling their issue first, as long as a human is behind it. 74% want it resolved without leaving the game. And 58% will quit over a bad support experience. Studios agree too: 80% see AI becoming the default for player support.
Their worry isn’t AI. It’s AI that doesn’t understand games. That’s the gap Keywords Studios’ AI-native platform, Helpshift, was built to close. One AI agent can handle a lot, but not everything. A billing query and a self-harm disclosure can’t share the same tone, rules or guardrails. See Care AI in action
Deck building
The biggest impact on Playstack has been developer perceptions of the company; perhaps inevitably, it has become cemented as ‘the Balatro publisher’ in the minds of many, which has in turn influenced the type of games it is pitched.
“Raccoin’s a really good example – they probably were inspired by Balatro,” says Elliott. “So Raccoin probably only existed because Balatro existed, and because we’d published Balatro, they had to bring it to us. So it created Raccoin in that way. We’ve had a surprising number of those parlor roguelike games being pitched to us, and we’ve got a couple more coming out. So yes, it sort of created a theme within the games, but that’s still a very small proportion of what we do – and really there only is one Balatro.”
It’s important to note that ‘the Balatro publisher’ is far from a one-hit wonder. Ten years in, the company has a hit rate of 85%, thanks to best-sellers such as Abiotic Factor, the Mortal Shell series, and mystery game The Case of the Golden Idol (plus its sequel and six DLCs).
“We are really proud of that,” says Elliott, “but the 15% is really important too, because if you only did things that were safe and profitable, you don’t take as many risks, and I don’t think indie publishing is about that. Indie publishing and development is about taking risks. It’s about having an idea that people just generally don’t quite see how [it would work], but it becomes phenomenal and captures people. 85% is a really nice number, maybe 70% would be brilliant too. But 100%, we’re probably making some mistakes in what we’re filtering out.”
He continues: “Indies can be quite fearless. Look at Color Gray Games and Case of the Golden Idol, which has a very distinctive 2D art aesthetic and a quite traditional old-school point and click-style gameplay... that could never be a AAA experience, because that’s a risk people have never taken, but it’s been really successful and led to a franchise.
“It could afford to be fearless because it didn’t have the world’s greatest expectation on it. With the bigger budgeted games, those risks are harder to take. You can still have exceptional games, but there is something quite refreshing about where indie games can go.”
New ownership, new opportunities
Mortal Shell 2 is the latest Playstack hit
Playstack is now in a position to take even more risks, thanks to some new owners.
Back in May, the publisher was acquired by Integrated Media Company (IMC), the owner of Fandom and GameSpot, valuing Playstack at £125 million (or, as Ellliott prefers to say, “one eighth of £1 billion”). The CEO emphasises that nothing will really change – he has no earn-out or escape clause, and remains “as committed as ever to the business” – but the deal enables the indie publisher to explore the big question: where does it go next?
“It’s healthy for us to have a slightly bigger investor group that we can talk to about things, about new directions and things we’d like to do as a business,” he explains. “Everything in games evolves, so we’ve got to keep evolving with it. And they love us for who we are, so that’s a good thing, too.”
He adds: “We had a business plan signed off with [previous owner] TruFin at the end of last year, and that’s the exact same business plan we’ve adopted with IMC – delivering the exact same number of games, the exact same revenue opportunities. What it will change is if we have bigger appetites for some things in the future, we’ve got a lot more headroom with titles we might want to get behind and how we want to support games.
“We didn’t really test the limits of that with TruFin. We had really great support from them, but we were getting close to being quite a significant majority share of their business. So for us, having more headroom is very useful and very important. But we’re not changing the standards, the game selection process that we use, the way the team has to be passionate and get behind a game, the forecasting methodology we use – all of those things are still true.”
Does this mean there may be bigger games in Playstack’s future? Potentially, but Elliott stresses that they need to “make sure the numbers make sense for everyone.” The developers deserve to be profitable, and Playstack won’t spend extortionate amounts of money if it delays the point when anyone is earning royalties.
“We might have an appetite for some bigger games, but only if the numbers stack up,” he tells us. “And there are some growth opportunities for us as a business, where we think we could do more, and that was already part of our business plan. The constraint is on us and our ambition, not on how much money’s in the bank and what we are thinking. I’m always going to make sure we’re profitable with a great growth plan, but sometimes you’re funding projects for two, three years out, so you want to make sure you’ve got the cash flow for that.”
“Balatro led to Raccoin and there’s two more that we’ll be announcing later this year”
Crucially, this leeway and Playstack’s ongoing success enables the publisher to continue expanding its portfolio. That 85% hit rate isn’t driven by any single type of title, and Elliott is keen to ensure that remains the case.
“We aren’t a genre team,” he says. “We do have some games which happen to resonate around certain genres. That just happens. We had Case Of and Rise Of The Golden Idol, and we now have another detective-esque game we’re going to announce later this year. Balatro led to Raccoin and there’s two more that we’ll be announcing later this year. But we’re really a variety publisher in that our taste as players is all sorts of games, and we want to be able to publish all sorts of games.
“The portfolio will look its best when it’s varied and interesting with a diversified mixture of games inside it, and that portfolio will only build if we’re successful in publishing great games from creative developers.”
He concludes: “You asked what Balatro has changed about Playstack? It told us we’re doing the right things. It gave us that spring in our step. It has given us the ability to fund more projects and back more games and invest in more titles.
“We never want to be gigantic. We never want to be [in a position of] ‘oh, another week, another Playstack game’. That’s not who we are. We probably have eight releases this year, which is quite a lot. It’s busy. It’s healthy.”

Indie publisher Playstack is celebrating its tenth anniversary, and yet the company’s name has arguably only been on everyone’s lips for a couple of years – thanks largely to poker-themed roguelike deckbuilder Balatro.

As with so many indie breakouts, the 2024 smash hit seemed to come from nowhere but Playstack CEO and founder Harvey Elliott says his team were confident long before the name ‘Balatro’ was making headlines.

“We knew we had something special,” he tells The Game Business Show. “Nobody knows how special that could have been, but there was such a buzz about the game, such excitement. We all had our dream forecasts for how the game might do – and we were all low.

Balatro not only provided Playstack with great success but also with valuable lessons; for example, Elliott believes the company could have created “a different kinds of moment” if it had released on PC, consoles and mobile simultaneously (as opposed to the latter arriving several months later).

“Those sort of lessons, like the launch planning, timing the game release, and getting it out there, and just little things about when you submit a game on multiple platforms all at once... We’ve done more complicated things since because of Balatro, but we didn’t necessarily do them all with Balatro first time. A multi-SKU release is complicated, especially with a solo dev driving the creative and driving the game.”

Sponsored Message

Players already trust AI to help them. The problem is that most AI in gaming wasn’t built to.

From Helpshift, a Keywords Studios platform

66% of players are comfortable with AI handling their issue first, as long as a human is behind it. 74% want it resolved without leaving the game. And 58% will quit over a bad support experience. Studios agree too: 80% see AI becoming the default for player support.

Their worry isn’t AI. It’s AI that doesn’t understand games. That’s the gap Keywords Studios’ AI-native platform, Helpshift, was built to close. One AI agent can handle a lot, but not everything. A billing query and a self-harm disclosure can’t share the same tone, rules or guardrails. Care AI lets you build specialist AI agents, each an expert where it matters, each handing off to a human when it should.

See Care AI in action

Deck building

The biggest impact on Playstack has been developer perceptions of the company; perhaps inevitably, it has become cemented as ‘the Balatro publisher’ in the minds of many, which has in turn influenced the type of games it is pitched.

“Raccoin’s a really good example – they probably were inspired by Balatro,” says Elliott. “So Raccoin probably only existed because Balatro existed, and because we’d published Balatro, they had to bring it to us. So it created Raccoin in that way. We’ve had a surprising number of those parlor roguelike games being pitched to us, and we’ve got a couple more coming out. So yes, it sort of created a theme within the games, but that’s still a very small proportion of what we do – and really there only is one Balatro.”

It’s important to note that ‘the Balatro publisher’ is far from a one-hit wonder. Ten years in, the company has a hit rate of 85%, thanks to best-sellers such as Abiotic Factor, the Mortal Shell series, and mystery game The Case of the Golden Idol (plus its sequel and six DLCs).

“We are really proud of that,” says Elliott, “but the 15% is really important too, because if you only did things that were safe and profitable, you don’t take as many risks, and I don’t think indie publishing is about that. Indie publishing and development is about taking risks. It’s about having an idea that people just generally don’t quite see how [it would work], but it becomes phenomenal and captures people. 85% is a really nice number, maybe 70% would be brilliant too. But 100%, we’re probably making some mistakes in what we’re filtering out.”

He continues: “Indies can be quite fearless. Look at Color Gray Games and Case of the Golden Idol, which has a very distinctive 2D art aesthetic and a quite traditional old-school point and click-style gameplay... that could never be a AAA experience, because that’s a risk people have never taken, but it’s been really successful and led to a franchise.

“It could afford to be fearless because it didn’t have the world’s greatest expectation on it. With the bigger budgeted games, those risks are harder to take. You can still have exceptional games, but there is something quite refreshing about where indie games can go.”

New ownership, new opportunities

Playstack is now in a position to take even more risks, thanks to some new owners.

Back in May, the publisher was acquired by Integrated Media Company (IMC), the owner of Fandom and GameSpot, valuing Playstack at £125 million (or, as Ellliott prefers to say, “one eighth of £1 billion”). The CEO emphasises that nothing will really change – he has no earn-out or escape clause, and remains “as committed as ever to the business” – but the deal enables the indie publisher to explore the big question: where does it go next?

“It’s healthy for us to have a slightly bigger investor group that we can talk to about things, about new directions and things we’d like to do as a business,” he explains. “Everything in games evolves, so we’ve got to keep evolving with it. And they love us for who we are, so that’s a good thing, too.”

He adds: “We had a business plan signed off with [previous owner] TruFin at the end of last year, and that’s the exact same business plan we’ve adopted with IMC – delivering the exact same number of games, the exact same revenue opportunities. What it will change is if we have bigger appetites for some things in the future, we’ve got a lot more headroom with titles we might want to get behind and how we want to support games.

“We didn’t really test the limits of that with TruFin. We had really great support from them, but we were getting close to being quite a significant majority share of their business. So for us, having more headroom is very useful and very important. But we’re not changing the standards, the game selection process that we use, the way the team has to be passionate and get behind a game, the forecasting methodology we use – all of those things are still true.”

Does this mean there may be bigger games in Playstack’s future? Potentially, but Elliott stresses that they need to “make sure the numbers make sense for everyone.” The developers deserve to be profitable, and Playstack won’t spend extortionate amounts of money if it delays the point when anyone is earning royalties.

“We might have an appetite for some bigger games, but only if the numbers stack up,” he tells us. “And there are some growth opportunities for us as a business, where we think we could do more, and that was already part of our business plan. The constraint is on us and our ambition, not on how much money’s in the bank and what we are thinking. I’m always going to make sure we’re profitable with a great growth plan, but sometimes you’re funding projects for two, three years out, so you want to make sure you’ve got the cash flow for that.”

“Balatro led to Raccoin and there’s two more that we’ll be announcing later this year”

Crucially, this leeway and Playstack’s ongoing success enables the publisher to continue expanding its portfolio. That 85% hit rate isn’t driven by any single type of title, and Elliott is keen to ensure that remains the case.

“We aren’t a genre team,” he says. “We do have some games which happen to resonate around certain genres. That just happens. We had Case Of and Rise Of The Golden Idol, and we now have another detective-esque game we’re going to announce later this year. Balatro led to Raccoin and there’s two more that we’ll be announcing later this year. But we’re really a variety publisher in that our taste as players is all sorts of games, and we want to be able to publish all sorts of games.

“The portfolio will look its best when it’s varied and interesting with a diversified mixture of games inside it, and that portfolio will only build if we’re successful in publishing great games from creative developers.”

He concludes: “You asked what Balatro has changed about Playstack? It told us we’re doing the right things. It gave us that spring in our step. It has given us the ability to fund more projects and back more games and invest in more titles.

“We never want to be gigantic. We never want to be [in a position of] ‘oh, another week, another Playstack game’. That’s not who we are. We probably have eight releases this year, which is quite a lot. It’s busy. It’s healthy.”

title: Sensor Tower 2026年8月全球手游收入与下载量排行榜 TOP 10
author: Sensor Tower
text:
根据 Sensor Tower 应用表现洞察最新数据，《 王者荣耀 》在8月继续领跑全球手游收入榜。在中国市场，游戏于8月8日至15日期间推出“夏日农友节”和“无尽之局平行世界”两大重磅活动。此次更新不仅推出了新英雄“卢雅那”，还上线限时玩法“超极限狂潮”，通过缩短技能冷却时间、提供可叠加升级效果，并配合免费抽奖、全新外观及活动专属奖励，通过多样化玩法与奖励机制持续刺激玩家参与和付费。
《 Gossip Harbor 》在8月同样展现出亮眼表现，这主要得益于其节奏合理的运营活动规划。“Water Wonders（水上奇观）”和“Dollhouse of Dreams（梦幻娃娃屋）”将7月积累的热度延续至8月上半月；随后推出的“四周年庆典（Fourth-Year Festivities）”围绕周年主题设置合成任务和专属奖励，进一步丰富了游戏内容。进入8月下旬，龙族救援剧情活动“Slay the Dragon, Save the Day!（屠龙救援行动）”继续吸引玩家参与；“Escape from Raccoon Beach（逃离浣熊海滩）”和秋季主题活动“The Turning Leaves（秋叶流转）”则带来新的收集任务，并将活动延续至9月。
其他头部收入产品同样依靠持续推出的主题活动维持用户参与度与付费意愿。《 Whiteout Survival 》在8月推出内容丰富的活动矩阵，其中与《Kingshot》的联动成为当月重点。核心活动“Twin Star Adventure（双星历险记）”以北极熊探险为主题，结合了剧情和合作玩法；“State of Power（最强王国）”和“Winter Siege（冬日攻城战）”等联盟竞赛，则让玩家持续参与团队竞争。《 Royal Match 》于8月推出“Dragon Nest（龙之巢穴）”以及限时竞赛“Lightning Rush（闪电冲刺）”，进一步丰富了合作与竞技玩法。《 Candy Crush Saga 》则通过节奏有序的内容更新维持玩家热度，先后推出“Bubblegum Season（泡泡糖赛季）”、多轮赛事“Candy Cup 2026（糖果杯2026）”，并在8月底上线“Music Season（音乐赛季）”。
完整手游收入 TOP 10 榜单请参见上图。注：本文数据不包含第三方安卓渠道。
2026年8月，全球玩家在 App Store 和 Google Play 上的移动游戏支出达到65.7亿美元，环比下降1%。在市场份额方面，美国以28.6%的总收入占比继续保持全球领跑地位；中国（仅统计 iOS 端）以16.7%紧随其后；日本则以12.2%位列第3。
在全球手游收入增长榜中，回合制 RPG《 Fate/Grand Order 》位居第1名。其增长主要由日本市场推动，游戏在8月创下2026年以来的单月收入新高。11周年庆典为玩家带来每日登录奖励、全新任务、特别挑战以及以新角色“阿兹拉伊勒的哈桑”为核心的限时卡池。随后上线的年度“泳装活动2026”进一步推出夏日主题外观与全新可收集角色，推动玩家付费热度延续至9月初。
在8月全球手游收入增长榜前十名中，腾讯旗下或由腾讯发行的产品占据五席。其中，《 金铲铲之战（Teamfight Tactics） 》和《 无畏契约（VALORANT） 》分别位列第2名和第3名，增长主要来自中国市场。《金铲铲之战》推出全新“自然之力”赛季，带来新的角色和策略选择，并同步上线可自由切换双形态的卓越级英雄“不朽格温”。《无畏契约》则在手游上线一周年之际推出两套主题武器系列，分别是融入中国传统艺术元素的“墨武（Ink Warrior）”以及以花卉为设计主题的“千灵华绽（Thousand Spirits）”。
《 和平精英（Game for Peace） 》、《 英雄联盟手游（League of Legends: Wild Rift） 》和《 三角洲行动（Delta Force） 》同样实现榜单排名上升。《和平精英》推出来自国产动画《吞噬星空》的联动角色、武器与载具；《英雄联盟手游》将四周年庆典奖励与全新“水晶玫瑰2026”系列角色皮肤相结合；《三角洲行动》则通过“宝藏月”活动鼓励玩家持续登录、完成对局并搜寻高价值游戏藏品。这些活动表明，腾讯通过重磅版本更新、周年庆典、热门娱乐 IP 联动以及限定外观，为玩家创造持续回流和付费的动力。
新作《 Zeus: The God of Arrogance 》位列全球手游收入增长榜第10名。自8月下旬上线以来，该作持续稳居韩国手游收入榜榜首。作为 Com2uS Holdings 发行的竞技 MMORPG，游戏通过大规模战斗、职业化作战体系以及面向不同成长阶段玩家的竞技玩法，对希腊神话进行重新演绎。此外，游戏还设有离线成长系统，使角色能够在玩家离线期间继续发展；以制造为核心的职业则可以生产专属道具，为长期成长体系与游戏内经济提供支撑。
总体来看，8月榜单显示，头部手游的商业化越来越依赖持续且有层次的 Live Ops，而非单一大型活动。大型版本、周年庆和 IP 联动负责制造阶段性峰值，高频奖励、限时玩法与外观内容则承担承接热度和延长生命周期的作用。与此同时，快速崛起的新作也证明，定位清晰且时机适当的产品仍有机会在竞争激烈的市场中实现突破。欢迎通过 Sensor Tower 旗下 Playliner 运营活动洞察平台 ，深入了解影响游戏商业化及玩家参与度的运营策略。
2026年8月全球手游下载排行榜 TOP 10
《 ROBLOX 》位居2026年8月全球手游下载榜榜首，《 Free Fire 》排名第2。《 Block Blast! 》、《 Subway Surfers 》和《 Arrow Puzzle: Tap Puzzle Games 》紧随其后，共同跻身全球下载榜前五。
《 ROBLOX 》登顶全球手游下载榜，主要得益于其在8月推出的多元化精选体验。其中既包括 MMORPG《Vesteria》和战术 FPS《TTK》，也包括《Dress to Impress》与《Tower Defense Simulator》的大型版本更新。新上线的《Duck Duck》则进一步为平台补充了社交派对玩法。角色扮演、射击、时尚、策略与休闲等多品类内容的持续更新，不仅拓展了 Roblox 的用户吸引力，也帮助平台维持玩家关注度。
《 Free Fire 》在8月继续稳居全球手游下载榜第2名，延续了7月下旬结束的9周年庆典所带来的增长势头。在相对平静的月初过后，“Scarlet Moon（绯红之月）”于8月下旬在《Free Fire》及《Free Fire MAX》中同步上线，通过全新设计与专属奖励焕新经典收藏内容。游戏的持续强劲表现，反映出其稳定的全球吸引力，以及周年庆典活动所带来的长尾增长效应。
《 Subway Surfers 》在8月全球手游下载榜上环比上升三位，排名第4。“Fantasy Fest（奇幻庆典）”世界巡回更新为游戏带来充满魔法色彩的全新场景、新角色和限时挑战，其中还包括提供收集奖励的开学季活动。8月下旬上线的“Cosmic Crossroads（宇宙十字路口）”则将游戏舞台转移至太空主题环境，并加入全新角色、赛季奖励路线，以及回归的《Among Us》联动。主题地点、收集角色、挑战活动及跨界内容的持续轮换，不仅保持了游戏的新鲜感，也进一步吸引新老玩家参与。
2026年8月，全球手游下载量达到37.6亿次，环比增长1%。在国家与地区方面，印度以6.14亿次下载（占比16.4%）继续领跑全球；美国（7.4%）和巴西（5.8%）分别位列第2和第3位。
开放世界犯罪题材成为8月手游下载市场的一大亮点，两款快速崛起的新作引领了这一趋势。《 Gangstar Mirage City 》位居全球手游下载增长榜第1名，并在8月20日于多个市场上线后跻身全球下载总榜第7名。该作由腾讯旗下 Level Infinite 和 Gameloft 合作推出，玩家可以探索未来都市、自定义载具、建立犯罪帝国，并参与抢劫行动与帮派战斗。《 Gangster Miami RP: Grand City 》则位列下载增长榜第6名，为玩家提供由城市探索、驾驶及犯罪主题任务组成的类似体验。
两款游戏的下载增长主要来自印度、印度尼西亚、巴基斯坦和巴西等市场，这些市场本身拥有庞大的手游用户规模，且近期增长较快。两款新作的崛起也反映出，移动端开放世界犯罪题材仍具较强吸引力。与此同时，备受期待的主机游戏《 Grand Theft Auto VI 》也持续受到关注，进一步凸显了开放世界犯罪题材的市场热度。8月底，Rockstar Games 发布了《 Grand Theft Auto VI 》的加长版预告片，为游戏11月19日发售进一步预热。
新作《 Mystery Dumpling: Unbox ASMR 》位列全球手游下载增长榜第2名，并在8月上线后跻身全球下载总榜第12名。该游戏由 Brocker Bus Studio 发行，是一款将神秘盒拆封、ASMR 互动体验与色彩鲜明的卡通画面相结合的超休闲游戏。该作上线首月下载量超过1,100万次，其中印度尼西亚、巴西和土耳其贡献主要增量。
载具题材游戏在8月同样获得增长动能，《 Bus Fever-Car Jam Escape 》、《 Dear Passengers 》和《 Wheelie Master: Moto Ride 3D 》均进入全球手游下载增长榜前十。三款产品分别围绕巴士分类解谜、客运航空模拟以及摩托车特技驾驶展开，为交通运输题材提供了不同的休闲玩法。它们在印度、印度尼西亚、巴西、墨西哥和土耳其等高下载量市场表现突出，也说明简单易懂的载具玩法依然能够吸引大量玩家。
总体来看，8月全球手游下载榜既体现了成熟头部产品的持久生命力，也展现出新作及成长型产品的快速增长。高频内容更新帮助领先产品持续保持市场曝光，而开放世界犯罪、ASMR、解谜和载具模拟等易于上手的玩法，则在多个高下载量移动游戏市场获得较快增长。
